title: Induction cooktop: the coil, heat-proof glass, IGBTs and heatsink
summary: An induction cooktop has a flat copper work coil with ferrite bars, a heat-proof glass top, one or two 1,200 V IGBTs and a bridge rectifier on a heatsink, big film capacitors and a blower fan. Allow about 30 minutes. The capacitors can still hold a charge after unplugging: discharge them and prove them empty before you touch the board.

steps.text: Check whether it is worth keeping whole. A cooker that only needs a fuse, a cord or a new plug is worth more working: induction cooks with no flame, no fumes and very little wasted heat. It needs a magnetic pan (a magnet sticks to the base) and 1.5-2 kW, so a battery inverter must be big enough. Strip it only if it is dead.

Unplug it at the wall, and remove the cord from the unit if it comes off. A built-in hob is wired in: switch off and tag its breaker and prove the terminals dead with a meter (see safety_mains_isolation), then lift it out of the worktop with a helper. Wait at least 10 minutes before opening.
steps.warn: A hard-wired hob runs on 230 V or two phases at up to 7 kW. Never assume it is dead because the lights are off.

steps.text: Lay the unit glass-down on a folded towel on a flat bench. Take the screws out of the underside (some are security screws) and lift the base cover off. Photograph the board before you move anything.

Look before you touch. Find the capacitors: two rectangular film capacitors (about 0.3 µF, 1,200 V) beside the coil leads, and the DC filter capacitor (a cylinder or a larger film box). Note which parts are on the heatsink: the IGBTs and the rectifier.
steps.warn: The heatsink, board and many parts are wired straight to the mains with no isolation. Touch none of them until the capacitors have been discharged and measured.

steps.text: Discharge every large capacitor with the resistor tool from safety_discharge_capacitor. Use the chain of high-voltage resistors for the 1,200 V film capacitors: touch both terminals for at least 10 seconds. Then measure DC volts across each capacitor, and from each terminal to the heatsink: it should read under 1 V. Clip a jumper across each capacitor while you work.
steps.warn: Never short a capacitor with a screwdriver. Treat every capacitor as charged until the meter shows near zero.

steps.text: Take the coil. Unscrew the two thick coil leads from the board, then lift the coil out of its holder. It sits on a plastic or mica disc with ferrite bars glued or clipped underneath; free them gently, they are brittle. Take the small spring-loaded temperature sensor (NTC thermistor) from the centre of the coil with its wires.

Take the glass. A portable cooker's glass is held by silicone around the edge or by clips; slide a thin knife under the rim and lift it off flat. Check the edges and corners: a chip can grow into a crack. Wear gloves and carry it flat.
steps.warn: Ceramic glass breaks into sharp shards, and a chipped edge can fail suddenly with no warning.

steps.text: Remove the heatsink once the capacitors have been proved empty. Unscrew the clamp that holds the IGBTs and the bridge rectifier to it and unplug the fan. Keep them on the heatsink if you want, or desolder them. Photograph the part numbers on the IGBTs first.

Take the rest: the film capacitors, the DC-bus choke, the ceramic fuse and the mains cord with its plug (cut 15 cm back from the unit). Desolder carefully. Twist a bare wire across each capacitor's terminals before storing it.

Test what you took. Fuse and coil: continuity (see test_continuity); the coil should read near zero ohms. IGBTs and rectifier: diode test; a part that reads near zero in both directions between its main pins is shorted and dead. Film capacitors: capacitance meter (see test_capacitor). Fan: 12-18 V from a battery.

notes:
## What's worth keeping and why

- **Work coil.** A flat pancake of Litz wire (many fine insulated strands), about 15-20 cm across, with its ferrite bars. Litz wire is the right wire for high-frequency coils, and the coil with its ferrite is the heart of any induction heater.
- **Ceramic glass.** Heat-proof to several hundred degrees and flat. A good window for a stove, an oven or a solar oven (build_solar_oven). Don't cut it; keep it whole. Warm it gradually.
- **IGBTs (about 1,200 V, 15-40 A) and bridge rectifier.** Fast power switches and a mains rectifier on a ready-made heatsink. Useful in an inverter, a motor drive or a welder repair; check part numbers online if you can.
- **Film capacitors.** 1,200 V resonant capacitors: rarely easy to replace. Test and keep with their coil.
- **DC-bus choke, fuse, fan, heatsink, thermistor.** All standard parts.

## Reusing the board

- The board makes its own high frequency from rectified mains with no isolation. Don't run it open on the bench; if you want to reuse it as an induction heater, keep it whole in its case with its coil and sensor.
- Cookers with a coil that has cracked or lost its insulation: keep the ferrite, not the coil.

## Variations

- Built-in hobs have 2-5 coils, bigger boards and 230 V or two-phase supplies; the same steps apply. Take extra care with the mains.
- Portable units often use a single IGBT.
- A cooker that beeps and shows an error is often missing its pan or has a bad thermistor: check before you strip.
